title: Deficiency sets and hypersimplicity

based_on.title: Lecture notes in Computability Theory
based_on.pages: Proposition 17.1, pp. 37–38; Definition 34.3 and Proposition 34.4(1)–(3), p. 79; Proposition 34.5, p. 80

summary: Turn an injective enumeration of a noncomputable c.e. set into a hypersimple set of the same Turing degree, and distinguish hypersimplicity from simplicity.
abstract: An enumeration without repetitions may still present smaller numbers long after larger ones. Mark each position whose value is later undercut. These marks form an enumerable set carrying exactly the same information as the original range: either set can decide membership in the other using an oracle. If that range is noncomputable, the unmarked positions escape every computable sequence of disjoint finite tests. The marked set is therefore hypersimple, meaning that it is enumerable and its infinite complement is hyperimmune. This construction gives a hypersimple representative in every nonzero enumerable Turing degree, while keeping separate the properties of a set, its complement, and their shared degree. The earlier Post simple set provides the contrasting example: its complement has a computably bounded increasing enumeration, so that same set is not hypersimple.
